passage.title: Three wet nights in Snowdonia
passage.text:
Last summer my cousin Freya and I went camping in Snowdonia for three nights. Before that trip, neither of us (1) ____ ever slept in a tent, so we were very excited.

Unfortunately, it was pouring with rain when we reached the campsite. The tent was much smaller (2) ____ it looked in the photo online, and it took us ages to put it up in the wind. When we finally got inside, we realised it wasn't big (3) ____ for both of us and our bags, so we left them in the car.

That evening Freya discovered she had left (4) ____ own raincoat at home, so she had to borrow mine whenever she went outside. It was (5) ____ a cold night that we slept in our jumpers and woolly hats. Mud got everywhere, so we took (6) ____ our boots before climbing into the tent.

On the third morning, the sun came out. We dried everything on a fence, climbed a hill and had a picnic with amazing views across the valley. Looking back, the rain is the part we laugh about most, and we are already planning our next trip.

passage.text:
Woman: So, Daniel, have you decided what you're doing after school next term? Are you staying in the swimming team?
Daniel: No, I've done that for three years and I want a change. Jake asked me to join the basketball club, but it's on Thursdays and I've got guitar then.
Woman: What about tennis? Your cousin loves it.
Daniel: Actually, that's what I've signed up for. The lessons are on Tuesdays, so it's perfect.

Woman: Hi Ben, it's Karen from the football club. Just a quick message about Saturday's match against Hillside. Last week I told everyone it would start at half past nine, but their pitch is being used in the morning, so we've moved it to eleven. Please don't be late, though, because the coach wants the girls there an hour early, at ten, to warm up. See you then!

Woman: Attention, please, all members of the junior swimming team. The competition against Riverside Swimming Club, which was planned for Saturday the fourteenth, can't take place on that day, because the pool is needed for a diving event. We asked about the Friday evening, but too many of you are on school trips then. So the competition will now be on Sunday the fifteenth, starting at two o'clock.

Man: That's a nice racket, Sophie. Is it new?
Sophie: Yes, I got it yesterday. In the sports shop in town it was sixty pounds, which I thought was far too much.
Man: So where did you get it?
Sophie: Online. It was fifty pounds on the website, but I had a voucher for fifteen pounds off, so in the end I only paid thirty-five.

Man: Hello, runners. This is Steve with a quick message about Wednesday. We usually meet outside the sports centre, but the car park there is closed for repairs this week. I thought about using the school car park instead, but it's locked in the evenings. So let's meet at the main gates of Victoria Park at six thirty. We'll do our normal five kilometres around the lake.

Hannah: Do you fancy going to watch something on Saturday, Matt? There's a cycling race through the town centre.
Matt: I saw that last year. It was over in about two minutes. They just rushed past us!
Hannah: True. There's the basketball final at the arena, but the tickets are really expensive.
Matt: My uncle's got two free tickets for the cricket at the county ground. It's a long day, but we could take a picnic.
Hannah: Lovely. Let's do that, then.

Amy: Are you coming to rugby training tomorrow, Leo?
Leo: Yes. Do I need to bring my shirt? I left it at your house last time.
Amy: Don't worry, my mum's washed it and I'll bring it for you. But the coach said we're playing on the grass pitch, so you'll need your boots, not your trainers.
Leo: OK. And water?
Amy: There's a drinks machine at the club now, so you don't need to bring any.

passage.text:
Hayley: Congratulations, Luke! I saw the list. You're the king in the school play!
Luke: Thanks. I wanted to be the king's servant, actually. He's got all the funny lines.
Hayley: But the king's the main part!
Luke: I know, and that's the problem. I've got so many lines to learn and only five weeks. The singing's fine, I've done that before, but I don't know how I'll remember all those words.

Megan: Have you heard? From next month, we can't use our phones at all during the school day, not even at lunch.
Ravi: Yes. I think it's going to be good, actually. People will talk to each other more at break.
Megan: Maybe. But nobody asked us what we thought. The head teacher just decided. They should have had a vote in the school council.
Ravi: You're right about that. We're the ones who have to live with it.
Megan: Well, I'll find it hard. I check my phone all the time.

Jamie: How did the maths exam go, Priya? You were really nervous this morning.
Priya: I know! I hardly slept. But honestly, it was fine. The questions were the same kind we did in class, and I had loads of time at the end to check everything.
Jamie: Lucky you. I didn't even get to the last page.
Priya: Oh no. Well, I was sure I'd find it really hard, so I'm just glad it's over.

Rosie: How can you revise with music on, Adam? I need total silence.
Adam: I know, but silence doesn't work for me. If it's too quiet, I start thinking about other things.
Rosie: You could go to the library with Kim and Leo.
Adam: I tried that last week. They spent the whole time chatting, so I didn't get anything done. No, I'll stay in my room with my headphones on. I remember things much better that way.

Zoe: Mrs Taylor, have you got a minute? It's about the history project.
Mrs Taylor: Of course, Zoe. Are you finding it hard to choose a topic?
Zoe: No, I'm doing the history of the town market. I've already started. The thing is, you put me in a group with Ellie and Ben, and they want to do something completely different.
Mrs Taylor: I see.
Zoe: So I wondered if I could do it on my own. I don't mind doing all the work myself, and I can still finish by the end of the month.

Woman: How was the trip to the science museum, Owen?
Owen: Well, you know I didn't want to go. I thought it'd be really boring, just looking at old machines.
Woman: And was it?
Owen: Not at all! There were loads of things you could try yourself, and a guide showed us how robots are built. The coach journey took ages, but I'd go again tomorrow.
Woman: Mr Evans organised it very well, then.
Owen: Yes, everything happened exactly on time.

passage.text:
Woman: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Oakfield Wildlife Park. I'm Hannah, one of the rangers here, and I'd like to give you some useful information before you start exploring.

Woman: The park is very large, so most visitors use our little train, which goes all the way round. It leaves from the main entrance every twenty minutes, and if you stay on for the whole trip, it takes about forty minutes. You can get on and off as many times as you like.

Woman: Now, a lot of people go straight to see the bears, because they're our most famous animals. But my advice is to visit the wolves first. They're much more active in the morning, and by lunchtime they're usually asleep in the long grass, so you won't see very much.

Woman: At two o'clock every day, one of the keepers gives a short talk about the animals. In previous years the talk took place down by the lake, but this summer it's in the old barn, just behind the café, so you'll stay dry even if it rains.

Woman: We do ask you not to give the ducks on the lake any bread. Lots of children love doing it, but it's bad for the birds and can make them quite ill. If you'd like to feed them, special duck food is on sale at the kiosk.

Woman: You're welcome to bring your own lunch. There are picnic tables next to the playground, so parents can relax while the children play. Please don't eat in the car park, though, as it gets very busy.

Woman: Finally, for our younger visitors, there's a quiz sheet you can pick up at the entrance. Children who answer all the questions can collect a free badge from the gift shop. Last year we gave out pencils, but the badges, which have a picture of an otter on them, have been far more popular. Have a wonderful day!

Interviewer: My guest today is Maya Collins, who's only twenty-three but already has her photographs in several national magazines. Maya, welcome. How did you first get into photography?

Maya: Thanks for having me. Well, my grandfather gave me his old camera when I was fourteen. To be honest, I wasn't very excited about it at first. It was heavy and old-fashioned, and I mainly used it because I didn't want to hurt his feelings. But after a few weeks I realised I was looking at the world differently, noticing shadows and colours I'd never paid attention to before. That's what got me hooked.

Interviewer: And at seventeen you won a national competition. Did that change everything?

Maya: People always expect me to say yes, but it didn't really. The prize money was nice, and I bought a better lens with it. And no, magazines didn't suddenly start phoning me either. What really mattered was that one of the judges wrote to me afterwards with some very honest comments about the weak points in my pictures. It wasn't easy to read, but I learnt more from that letter than from winning the prize.

Interviewer: Nowadays almost everyone takes photos on their phone. Is that a problem for professional photographers like you?

Maya: Not at all. I know some photographers complain about it, but I think it's brilliant that everyone can take pictures now. Once people have tried to get a really good shot themselves, they understand how difficult it is, and they appreciate good photography more. I use my phone myself sometimes, actually, for quick ideas, though never for paid work.

Interviewer: What's the hardest part of your job?

Maya: Most people guess it's the early mornings, because the best light is just after sunrise. But I actually love being out at that time of day. And yes, my camera bag's heavy, but I've got used to that. No, what I find really tough is the waiting. Sometimes I stay in one place for a whole day for one particular picture, and it may never happen. I've learnt to take a good book with me!

Maya: I have mixed feelings. It's a great way for editors to find you. That's how I got my first magazine job. But I try very hard not to check how many likes a picture gets. When I used to do that, I started taking the kind of photos I thought people wanted, instead of ones I really cared about.

passage.title: A day with the otters and red pandas
passage.text:
My alarm goes off at half past five, which my friends think is crazy. But I need to be at Glenmore Wildlife Park, about twenty minutes' drive from Aberdeen, by seven o'clock, and the animals don't care whether it's raining or snowing. I'm Isla Grant, I'm twenty-three, and I've worked here as a keeper for two years, mainly with the red pandas and the otters.

The first job of the day is always the same: I walk round every enclosure and look carefully at each animal. You learn to notice small things, like an otter that isn't eating or a panda that stays inside when it usually comes out. If something seems wrong, I write it down and tell the vet. Visitors often imagine that keepers spend all day playing with the animals, but actually we try not to touch them much. They're wild animals, not pets, and we want them to behave as naturally as possible.

After the checks comes the part nobody talks about: cleaning. I spend at least two hours every morning washing floors, removing old food and changing water. It isn't exciting, but a clean enclosure stops diseases from spreading, so I don't mind it. Then I prepare the food. The otters eat fish, but the red pandas need mostly bamboo, and they're surprisingly fussy about it. If the leaves are even slightly old, they just leave them.

In the afternoon I give a short talk to visitors at the otter pool. When I started, I was terrified of speaking in front of a crowd, and my first few talks were a disaster. I'd learnt a script by heart and then forgot half of it. My manager suggested I forget the script and simply tell people stories about the animals instead. That changed everything. Now it's one of my favourite parts of the day, especially when children ask questions I can't answer.

People sometimes ask whether I wanted to be a zookeeper as a child. Honestly, I wanted to be a vet, but my exam results weren't good enough. I was disappointed for a while. Then I did a college course in animal care and spent a summer volunteering here, and at the end of it they offered me a job. I'm not paid much, and my back often hurts after lifting heavy bags of food. But last spring one of our red pandas had twins, and I was the first person to see them. At that moment I knew I wouldn't change this job for anything.

Last term I took part in my school's production of a musical called The Lighthouse. Our drama teacher, Mr Okafor, (1) ____ has written several plays himself, gave me the role of the old lighthouse keeper.

I was delighted, but I soon realised I had more than two hundred lines to learn (2) ____ heart. "You (3) ____ better start learning them today, or you won't be ready," Mr Okafor warned. So every evening my mum read the other characters' lines while I practised mine.

Rehearsals were hard work, but the cast became really close. We helped (4) ____ other with difficult scenes, and the older students gave us useful advice about staying calm on stage.

On the first night I was the (5) ____ nervous I have ever been: my hands were shaking and my mouth was completely dry. But as soon (6) ____ the curtain went up and I heard the audience laugh at my first joke, my nerves disappeared.

We performed the show three times, and every night the hall was full. I'm already hoping to get a part in next year's play.

passage.text:
Man: Your room looks great, Mia. The yellow's really bright. How long did it take you?
Mia: Well, I planned to do it all in a weekend, so two days. But on Saturday I spent the whole morning just moving the furniture and covering the floor. So I finished on Monday after school. Three days altogether.
Man: Not bad. It took me a week to paint the kitchen!

Woman: Hello, Josh, it's Gran. Are you still free on Saturday? I need some help in the garden.
Josh: Sure. Is it the apples again?
Woman: No, there weren't many this year, so I picked them myself. And Mr Lewis next door has offered to cut the hedge with his machine. But those big pots by the back door are much too heavy for me now, and I want to move them into the greenhouse before it gets cold.
Josh: No problem. I'll be there at ten.

Grace: Are you going to the garden centre, Paul? Can you get some red flowers for the pots by the front door?
Paul: I bought some last week, remember? They're still in the garage. I'm going because the handle's broken on the spade.
Grace: Oh yes. What about grass seed for that bare patch?
Paul: We've still got half a box of that. So it's just the spade, I think.

Man: Ollie, before your friends arrive this afternoon, there are a few things I need you to do.
Ollie: Like what?
Man: Well, the car needs washing, but that can wait until tomorrow. And the grass is getting long, but it's too wet to cut it today. Your bedroom, on the other hand, looks terrible, and your friends will be in there. So start with that, please.

Kate: Rob, I'm going to be home late tonight. I've got a meeting until eight.
Rob: OK. Shall I do the washing-up?
Kate: I'll do that when I get back, it's only a few plates. But tomorrow's rubbish day, and I always forget, so could you take the bins out before you go to bed?
Rob: Sure. Do you want me to iron your blue shirt for tomorrow?
Kate: No, thanks. I'm wearing a jumper.

Jenny: Mark, you know I couldn't find my keys this morning? I looked in my coat pocket three times, and I even went out to the garden shed, because I'd been in there yesterday.
Mark: And?
Jenny: They were by the washing machine! I must have put them down when I was doing the laundry.

Woman: Hello, this is Mrs Patel at number twelve, Elm Road. I'm calling about my kitchen. I rang last month about the window that wouldn't close, and your man fixed it very well, thank you. This time it's the tap. It won't turn off properly and it's dripping all day and all night. The fridge is making a strange noise too, but it's still keeping things cold, so that's not urgent. Could someone come on Thursday?

passage.text:
Becky: We've run out of milk again, and there's no bread either.
Joe: I know. We always forget something when we go to the supermarket.
Becky: Shall we write a list and put it on the fridge?
Joe: We tried that, remember? Nobody looked at it. Why don't we just order everything on the internet once a week? They bring it to the door, and the app remembers what we usually buy.
Becky: Hmm, OK. Let's try it.

Isla: Grandad, your apple cake is the best thing ever. How do you make it?
Grandad: It's my mother's recipe. I've never written it down. It's all in my head.
Isla: That's exactly why I'm asking! Will you show me on Sunday? I'll write everything down as we go, so it's never lost.
Grandad: Of course. Are you going to sell them at the school fair?
Isla: Maybe one day! But I just don't want the recipe to disappear.

Gemma: How was the Thai cooking class, Helen?
Helen: Well, the recipes were really easy. I could make them all at home now. But the chef just stood at the front reading from his notes. He didn't come round once to see how we were doing.
Gemma: Oh dear.
Helen: The other people were lovely, though. We're meeting for coffee next week. But I won't do another class with him.

Tom: Did you try that new Italian place on Mill Street, Jess?
Jess: Yes, on Friday. The pasta was amazing, honestly the best I've had in this town.
Tom: Great. I've heard it's quite cheap too.
Jess: It is, and you get loads on your plate. But we waited forty minutes for our main course, and the waiter got our drinks wrong twice.

Nadia: I've stopped eating meat, you know. Three months now.
Callum: Really? How's it going?
Nadia: Fine! And my shopping costs much less. Beans and lentils cost almost nothing compared to chicken.
Callum: That's true. My sister's vegetarian and she says the same. I'm not sure it's always healthier, though. Some veggie burgers are full of salt.
Nadia: Maybe. The worst thing is eating out. Most places only have one boring vegetarian dish.

Finn: Dad, can I make dinner tonight?
Man: You? That's a first! Is it for Mum's birthday or something?
Finn: No, that's next month. It's for food technology at school. We've got a cooking competition in two weeks, and we have to make a main course in an hour. So I want to try my recipe at home first and see how long it takes.
Man: Good idea.

passage.text:
Man: Hello, everyone. I'm Richard Bell, the director of the Castlegate Summer School here in York, and I'm going to tell you about this year's English course, which runs for three weeks in July.

Man: Let's start with accommodation. In the past, some students stayed in rooms at the college, but those rooms are being repaired this year, so everyone will be living with host families. All our families live a short bus ride from the school.

Man: Lessons take place in the mornings, from Monday to Friday. There are four lessons each morning, and each one lasts fifty minutes, with a break for a drink and a snack in the middle.

Man: In the afternoons, you can choose from a range of activities. Many students expect football to be the favourite, but in fact drama is always the most popular. Some of our drama students have gone on to act in plays back home.

Man: Every Saturday there's a full-day trip. Last year our first trip was to a museum in Leeds, but this year we're starting with a visit to a castle on the coast, which last year's students voted for.

Man: Now, what should you pack? You don't need to bring towels or sheets, because your host family will provide them. But please do pack a raincoat. Even in summer, the weather here can change very quickly.

Man: And finally, on the last evening of the course, we hold a party in the school garden, and that's when you'll receive your certificate. Your host families are very welcome to come along too. I'm looking forward to meeting you all.

passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Daniel Hughes, a vet who works in a small country practice in north Wales. Daniel, did you always want to be a vet?

Daniel: Not at all! As a child I was actually a bit frightened of dogs, and we didn't have any pets at home. I was quite good at science at school, but I wanted to be an engineer. Then, when I was fifteen, I spent a summer on my uncle's farm, and one night a cow was having trouble giving birth. The vet arrived, and an hour later the mother and the calf were both fine. I remember thinking: that's what I want to do.

Interviewer: What surprised you when you started working?

Daniel: Everyone had warned me how hard the studying would be, and they were right, but I was ready for that. And I knew the hours would be long. What I hadn't expected was how much of the job is talking to people. Owners are often upset or worried, and you need to explain things calmly and kindly. That's something nobody really teaches you at university.

Interviewer: Which part of the job do you enjoy most?

Daniel: People imagine I'd love the puppy appointments best, and of course puppies are lovely. Operations can be exciting, too. But what I really enjoy is driving out to the farms and being outside, even when it's pouring with rain. Every day's different out there, and the farmers are great to work with.

Interviewer: Do you have to work at night?

Daniel: Yes, about twice a week I'm on call. I won't pretend it's easy. I'm often very tired the next day. But it's part of being a vet, and I accept that. And there's something quite special about helping a lamb into the world at three in the morning.

Interviewer: Lots of pet owners look things up online before they come to see you. Does that annoy you?

Daniel: Some of my colleagues get quite annoyed, but I don't. It shows that people care about their animals. The trouble is that they often read about the worst possible illness, so they arrive much more worried than they need to be. Usually it's something quite simple.

Interviewer: And what about the future? Would you like your own practice one day?

Daniel: A couple of friends from university have opened their own practices in the city, and people often ask if I'll do the same. But I'm really happy where I am, and the paperwork that comes with running a business doesn't appeal to me at all. What I would like, though, is to teach vet students part-time one day. I had some brilliant teachers, and I'd love to do that for someone else.

Interviewer: Daniel Hughes, thank you.

passage.title: The year that changed me
passage.text:
Ten years ago, when I was sixteen, I left my home in Leicester to spend a school year in a small town in northern Norway on an exchange programme. I'm now a teacher myself. My students often ask me about doing something similar, and I always say yes. But I also tell them it won't be what they expect.

I'd chosen Norway mostly because of the mountains in the photos. I hadn't thought much about the language, and I arrived knowing only 'hello' and 'thank you'. My host family, the Larsens, spoke excellent English, which was a relief at first. The problem was that I used it as an excuse. For the first two months I hardly learnt any Norwegian, and at school I sat quietly at the back of lessons I couldn't follow.

Things changed in November, when the days became very short and dark. I felt lonely and seriously thought about going home. It was my host brother, Even, who noticed. He didn't give me any advice. Instead, he asked me to join his handball team, although I'd never played. Nobody spoke English during training, so I had no choice: I had to understand the instructions or get hit by the ball. Within a few weeks I was following conversations, and by Christmas I was making jokes, even if they were bad ones.

The other surprise was school itself. In England I'd been used to lots of homework and tests. In Norway, students called teachers by their first names and were expected to plan their own projects. At first I found this confusing. Nobody told me exactly what to do. But it taught me to organise my own time, which helped me a lot at university later.

The hardest moment was actually the end of the year. I'd expected to be excited about going home, but saying goodbye to the Larsens was awful, and back in England I felt strangely out of place for months. My old friends had moved on, and the stories I wanted to share didn't interest them much.

I still visit Norway every couple of years, and Even came to my wedding last summer. When people ask what I learnt that year, they expect me to say 'Norwegian'. That's true, of course. But the more important lesson was that feeling uncomfortable is often the first step towards something good.

Daniel Okafor

passage.title: How much is too much?
passage.text:
Ask any parent what worries them most about their teenage children, and many will give the same answer: screens. Phones, tablets, games consoles: young people seem to be looking at one of them almost all the time. (1) ________ According to one recent study of British 13- to 16-year-olds, the average is around seven hours a day, not counting schoolwork.

That number sounds shocking, but researchers say we should be careful with it. (2) ________ A teenager might be listening to music, chatting to friends and watching a video at the same moment, and each activity is counted separately.

Not all screen time is the same, either. Dr Ellen Ward, who studies young people's sleep, believes the problem is not how long teenagers spend online but when. (3) ________ The bright light tells the brain that it is still daytime, and messages that arrive late at night keep teenagers awake.

Some schools have decided to act. At Riverside Academy in Belfast, students hand in their phones when they arrive and get them back at four o'clock. (4) ________ Now, says head teacher Ciaran Doyle, most of them say they prefer it, because break times have become far more sociable.

Teenagers themselves are not always happy with the way adults talk about the subject. Sixteen-year-old Maya told us that her phone is how she keeps in touch with her cousins in Canada and how she learns the guitar from online videos. (5) ________

Perhaps, then, the real question is not simply how many hours teenagers spend on screens, but what they use those hours for.

passage.title: My first time on a climbing wall
passage.text:
For my fifteenth birthday, my friend Priya and I decided to try the new indoor climbing wall in Leeds. I was a bit nervous because I'm (1) ____ of heights, but Priya persuaded me to come.

First, an instructor called Dan showed us how to put on our harnesses and tie the ropes correctly. He also (2) ____ sure that we understood the safety rules before we started.

The wall was covered in brightly coloured holds, and each colour showed a different (3) ____ of difficulty. We began with the easy yellow route. Priya reached the top in less than two minutes, but halfway up I made the mistake of looking down, and my legs started shaking. Dan shouted from the ground, "Don't (4) ____ up now - you're nearly there!" His words gave me the confidence to continue, and when I finally touched the top, I felt really proud.

By the end of the session my arms were aching, but I had (5) ____ a lot of fun. Priya and I have already (6) ____ another session for next Saturday, and this time I want to try the blue route.

passage.title: The woman next door
passage.text:
A few weeks ago, a woman moved into the empty flat next to ours in Manchester. For several days I only saw her carrying boxes up the stairs, so one afternoon my dad and I baked some biscuits and knocked on her door.

She introduced herself as Ines, a woman (1) ____ family had come to England from Portugal when she was a child. She told us that she lives by (2) ____, but that her two grown-up sons visit her every weekend. "(3) ____ of them play in a jazz band," she said proudly.

"Where (4) ____ you live before?" my dad asked. "In a tiny flat above a shop," she answered. "It was so noisy that I could hardly sleep!"

It soon turned (5) ____ that Ines was a piano teacher, and she offered to give me some free lessons. Now I go round every Thursday after school. She is patient and funny, and she gets on well (6) ____ everyone in our building, even the grumpy man on the top floor.

I'm really glad we knocked on her door that day.

passage.text:
Man: Hello, it's Peter Brown. I've got an appointment with Dr Shah on Friday at eleven.
Woman: Yes, Mr Brown, I can see it here.
Man: Well, I've just found out I have to work on Friday. I don't want to cancel it completely, because I still need to talk to her about my blood test results. Is there anything on Monday instead?
Woman: Let me see. Yes, Monday at nine twenty.

Woman: Hello, this is a message for Mrs Clarke from Bridge Street Dental Practice. It's about your son Harry's check-up. It was booked for Tuesday afternoon, but unfortunately the dentist is away that day. We could offer Monday morning at nine, but I know Harry's at school then, so we've put him in on Thursday at a quarter past four instead. Please call us if that's a problem.

Woman: Well, Mr Hughes, your knee isn't broken, you'll be pleased to hear.
Man: That's good. Should I keep it up on a chair and not walk on it?
Woman: No, not at all. That's what people used to do, but now we know it gets better more quickly if you move it. I'll give you a sheet with some simple exercises to do three times a day. You can take painkillers if you really need them, but try not to.

Man: Hello, Ella. What can I do for you today?
Ella: Well, I fell off my bike on Saturday. I thought I'd hurt my wrist, but it's fine now.
Man: Good.
Ella: The problem is my ear. It's been really painful since Sunday, and I can't hear very well on this side.
Man: Any cough or sore throat?
Ella: No, nothing like that.

Woman: Your teeth look very healthy, Ryan. I can tell you're not eating too many sweets.
Ryan: My mum doesn't let me!
Woman: Good for her. But you're missing the ones at the back when you brush. Try to spend two minutes on it, not thirty seconds.
Ryan: OK. Do I need to come back soon?
Woman: No, I'll see you in a year.

Sam: What time's your appointment at the hospital tomorrow, Laura?
Laura: Half past ten. I was going to drive, but you can never find anywhere to park there.
Sam: I could take you.
Laura: You're working, Sam! It's fine. The number fourteen bus stops right outside the hospital, and it's much cheaper than a taxi. I'll just leave a bit early.

Man: Good morning. Can I have your name, please?
Anna: Anna Kowalski. I'm here to see the nurse at ten.
Man: Ah, yes. The nurse is usually in Room Three, just down there, but it's being painted this week. So she's upstairs today, on the first floor, in Room Eight. You can take the lift if you like. Room Twelve, on the second floor, is the doctor's room, so don't go up that far.

passage.text:
Jordan: Did you watch Star Search last night?
Molly: Of course. That girl from Cardiff was amazing. I think the singers are much better than last year.
Jordan: Really? I thought last year's were just as good. But the judges! Did you hear what they said to that old man?
Molly: Yes, that was horrible. They didn't need to laugh at him like that.
Jordan: Exactly. They should tell people what's wrong in a nicer way.

Sara: So, for your birthday, there's that musical at the Grand Theatre.
Neil: I'm not a big fan of musicals, you know that. What else is on?
Sara: There's a comedy night at the Arts Centre, and a modern dance show.
Neil: Comedy would be fun.
Sara: It's sold out, I'm afraid. I checked this morning.
Neil: Oh. Well, I've never seen modern dance. Let's try something new.
Sara: Great, I'll book it.

Kyle: How was the Midnight Sky concert, Freya?
Freya: The band were fantastic. They played all my favourite songs.
Kyle: So you had a great time?
Freya: Not really. There were so many people that I couldn't move, and it was so hot. I spent half the time worrying about getting out. Next time I'll get a seat upstairs, even if I can't see as well.

Amira: Are you coming to the Riverside Festival with us, Tyler? Everyone's going.
Tyler: I'd love to. The bands are great this year.
Amira: So book a ticket!
Tyler: It's ninety pounds, plus the train. I've only just started my Saturday job and I'm saving for a laptop. I'll see how much I've got at the end of the month.
Amira: The camping's free, if that helps.
Tyler: That's good, but sleeping in a tent isn't my favourite thing.

Woman: I didn't know you played the guitar, Noah. How long have you been learning?
Noah: About a year. My parents always wanted me to learn the piano, but I wasn't interested.
Woman: So what changed?
Noah: My friend Dev started a band with some boys from school, and they needed a guitarist. I really wanted to be in it, so I asked for lessons for my birthday. We do music at school too, but it's only singing.

Lauren: Well, what did you think?
Aaron: Most of it was brilliant. I loved the way the story kept jumping between the past and now.
Lauren: Did you? I got a bit lost in the middle.
Aaron: No, it was clear enough. And two and a half hours went really quickly. But after all that, the last five minutes were so silly! Everyone suddenly became friends and everything was fine. I expected something much cleverer.

passage.text:
Woman: Hello, everyone. I'm Mrs Okafor, and I teach food technology here at Millbrook School. I'm really pleased to tell you about our new after-school cooking club, which starts next week.

Woman: First of all, please note that the club will meet every Thursday. The poster in the corridor says Wednesday, but that's a mistake, and we'll be changing it soon.

Woman: Sessions start at quarter to four and finish at half past five. We'll be using the new kitchen behind the sports hall, not the old classroom near the library, which is too small for a big group.

Woman: The club costs two pounds a week. That money pays for all the ingredients, so you won't need to bring any food with you.

Woman: In our very first session, we were planning to make pizza. Unfortunately, one of the ovens is being repaired, so instead we'll be making soup, which we can cook on the hob. Don't worry, pizza will come later in the term!

Woman: We provide aprons, so you don't need to bring one. But please bring a plastic box with a lid each week, so that you can take home whatever you've made. Your families will be able to taste your cooking, too.

Woman: Finally, at the end of term, we'll hold a competition, and our head teacher has kindly agreed to be the judge. The winning recipe will appear in the school magazine. So, if you'd like to join, please put your name on the list outside my classroom by Friday.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
passage.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Owen Barker, a nineteen-year-old student who has just cycled right across France, from the north coast down to the Mediterranean. That's about twelve hundred kilometres. Owen, why did you decide to do it?

Owen: A lot of people assume I did it for charity, and I did collect a bit of money for a children's hospital, but that wasn't the main reason. I'd spent the whole year sitting in front of a screen, revising for exams, and I was desperate to do something physical, something completely different. My cousin Ben felt the same, so we went together.

Interviewer: How much planning did you do?

Owen: Far too much, I think now. We had every day organised: where we'd eat, where we'd sleep, how many kilometres we'd cover. Looking back, that was a mistake. Some of the best moments were in places we found by chance, when we got lost or took a different road. Next time I'll leave much more to chance.

Interviewer: What was the hardest part?

Owen: Before we left, I was worried about the hills, but they were fine. You just go slowly. And we had a couple of very wet days, which weren't much fun. No, the worst thing was when Ben got a stomach bug and we had to stay in a small town for three days. I felt so frustrated just sitting there, knowing how far we still had to go.

Interviewer: What about the people you met?

Owen: I was nervous before we went, because my French is terrible, and I thought people might be impatient with us. Actually, everyone was incredibly kind. One farmer let us put our tent up in his garden when the campsite was full, and his wife brought us breakfast in the morning! Hardly anyone spoke English, mind you, but we managed with our hands.

Interviewer: How did you feel when you finally reached the sea?

Owen: I'd imagined we'd be jumping up and down, celebrating. And we did take lots of photos on the beach. But honestly, I felt a bit sad more than anything. For three weeks, all we'd had to think about was cycling and eating, and suddenly it was over.

Interviewer: Would you recommend a trip like this to other students?

Owen: Definitely. People think you need to be really fit before you start, but we weren't, especially me. You get fitter every day. And you don't need an expensive bike. Mine was second-hand. The one thing I'd say is go with someone you get on well with, because you spend every minute together!

Interviewer: Owen Barker, thanks for coming in.

passage.title: Ready when the phone rings
passage.text:
On a wet Saturday evening in October, Rhys Evans was halfway through dinner with his family when his phone made a sound he knows very well. A walker had fallen on a mountain path above the village and couldn't stand up. Within ten minutes Rhys had left his food, put on his boots and was driving to the team's base.

Rhys, 38, runs a bicycle shop in north Wales. He is also one of around forty volunteers in the local mountain rescue team, and none of them is paid. 'People are often amazed when I tell them that,' he says. 'They imagine we're professionals working for the government. In fact, we're teachers, farmers, nurses, and one of us is a dentist.' The team depends on money from the public to buy everything from ropes to its two vehicles.

Rhys joined eight years ago, after he got lost himself. 'I'd gone up a mountain in trainers, without a map, and the cloud came down,' he remembers, smiling. 'I'm embarrassed about it now. The team found me in about an hour, and they didn't make me feel stupid at all. I decided I wanted to do the same for other people.'

Becoming a member wasn't quick. New volunteers train for about a year before they go out on real rescues, learning first aid, how to use ropes and how to find their way at night. Rhys admits he nearly gave up. 'I thought I was fit, but carrying a heavy stretcher down a steep hill in the rain is something else. I was always the slowest.' What kept him going, he says, was the support of the older members, who never criticised him.

The team is called out more than a hundred times a year, and the number is growing. Rhys believes social media is partly responsible. 'Someone posts a beautiful photo from the top of a mountain, and thousands of people want to go there. Many of them have no idea how quickly the weather can change.' However, he doesn't want people to stay away. 'We'd much rather people came well prepared, with warm clothes, a map and a charged phone, than not at all.'

That October night, the walker turned out to have a broken ankle. It took the team four hours to carry her down. Rhys got home after two in the morning and opened his shop as usual at nine. Is it worth it? 'Every time,' he says.

The experiment ended last December. The family did not manage to avoid plastic completely, because some things, such as medicines, were impossible to buy without it. passage.title: From brick to smartphone
passage.text:
Today almost everyone carries a mobile phone, but the first ones looked very different. In 1983, one of the earliest mobile phones (1) ____ on sale in the United States. It weighed nearly a kilogram, its battery lasted for (2) ____ thirty minutes, and it cost almost four thousand dollars.

During the 1990s, phones became smaller and cheaper, and people started sending text messages. At first, each message could only (3) ____ up to 160 characters, so users invented short forms like "CU L8R" for "see you later".

Man: So which one will you go to?
Lily: Well, Grandma's already paid for the lesson, so I'll do that and send Zara a present.

Woman: Did you go camping with your brother at the weekend, Alex?
Alex: That was the plan, but the weather was awful, so we stayed in town.
Woman: Oh no. What did you do instead?
Alex: Well, we wanted to go to the food festival in the park, but that was cancelled because of the rain as well. So we went to the transport museum. It was much better than I expected, actually.

Nina: So where shall we meet for the film tomorrow, Chloe?
Chloe: It starts at seven. Shall we meet outside the cinema at quarter to?
Nina: It's going to rain all evening, according to the forecast. Why don't we meet in the café next door? We can have a hot chocolate first.
Chloe: Good idea. I'm getting the bus, so I'll come straight from the bus station. See you there at half six.

Woman: You're not going to play that computer game all evening again, are you, Ethan?

Woman: So you're staying in?
Ethan: Yes, but the big match is on TV at eight, and I really want to see that. Can I invite Kieran round to watch it?

Rachel: I've booked tickets for the theme park in the half-term holiday.
Chris: Great. Did you get the family ticket?
Rachel: I looked at that, but it's only for two adults and two children, and we're taking your mum as well. And the one-day tickets were thirty pounds each! So I got the tickets for the whole year. They cost a bit more, but if we go twice, they're cheaper.

Man: And now some news for music fans. The Greenfield Music Festival is back in August, but not in its usual place by the river, because the field there is still too wet after the floods in the spring. The organisers wanted to use the beach, but the town council said no. So this year it'll be in the grounds of Harwood Castle, which is only a short bus ride from the town centre.

Woman: I can't believe you got tickets for the Blue Lights concert! They sold out online in ten minutes.
Dan: I know. I tried the website as soon as they went on sale, but it kept crashing. Then I thought about queuing at the box office, but people were there all night.
Woman: So how did you get them?
Dan: My friend Tariq won two in a radio competition, and he can't go, so he gave them to me.

Fiona: I read that we should all sleep eight hours a night. I'm lucky if I get six.
Dominic: Me too. I always look at my phone in bed, and then I'm awake for ages.
Fiona: Same here. I really think the screen keeps you awake. I'm going to leave mine in the kitchen.
Dominic: Good idea. Mind you, I went swimming yesterday and I still couldn't sleep.
Fiona: Really? Swimming always makes me sleep like a baby.

Gareth: How's the new gym, Olivia?
Olivia: The machines are all brand new, and it's only five minutes from my flat.
Gareth: Sounds perfect.
Olivia: It would be, but I can only go after work, and that's when everyone else goes. I usually have to wait ages to use anything. I might start going early in the morning instead.

Kirsty: Are you still cycling to work, Ian?
Ian: Every day. I thought it would take much longer than the car, but with all the traffic in the mornings, I actually get there ten minutes earlier.
Kirsty: Isn't it dangerous, though, on those busy roads?
Ian: There's a cycle path most of the way now, so I feel quite safe. And I'm not tired at all. I've got more energy than before.

Marcus: Since when do you do yoga, Holly?
Holly: Since January. My sister's been trying to get me to go with her for years, but I always said no.
Marcus: So what changed your mind?
Holly: Exams, really. I was so stressed I couldn't think properly. Someone told me yoga helps you relax, so I tried it. And it works. I feel much calmer now. My sister's really happy I'm there, of course!

Ruth: So, how's the no-sugar month going, Pete?
Pete: Well, I was sure I'd be desperate for chocolate after a couple of days. But honestly, I hardly think about it.
Ruth: Really? I'd find it impossible.
Pete: So did I! I haven't lost any weight yet, but that wasn't really why I did it. I just wanted to have more energy.

Woman: You've been out running every day this week, Max!
Max: It's this app. It gives you points for every kilometre, and you can see how your friends are doing. I'm trying to beat Lewis.
Woman: I thought you hated running.
Max: I did! But now it's like a game. And it was free, so you can't complain.

passage.text:
Man: Good morning. My name's Gareth Price, and I work for Hadley Town Council. I'm here to explain how our new bike-hire scheme works. It starts on the first of May.

Man: To begin with, there'll be fifteen places around Hadley where you can collect a bike. We're hoping to have thirty by next summer, so the scheme should grow quite quickly.

Man: Before you can hire a bike, you'll need to register. You can do this online, or, if you'd rather speak to someone, at the library on Market Street. Lots of people have asked about the town hall, but unfortunately you can't register there.

Man: The first thirty minutes of every journey are free. After that, you pay one pound for each hour, so an afternoon ride out into the countryside won't cost very much at all.

Man: All the bikes are bright green, and every one has a basket at the front, which is really useful if you're going shopping. They also have lights, so you can ride them safely after dark.

Man: We don't provide helmets, I'm afraid. But we strongly recommend wearing one, and you can buy a cheap one at the cycle shop inside the railway station.

Man: Finally, if anything's wrong with your bike, a flat tyre, for example, please return it to a stand and press the red button. That tells our team it needs repairing. The green button is only for unlocking the bike. Happy cycling!

passage.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Priya Shah, who taught English in Leeds for five years before moving to Chile, where she now works in a secondary school in the city of Valparaíso. Priya, why did you decide to move abroad?

Priya: People often ask if I went for the money, but actually I earn less now than I did in England. And no, I didn't follow a boyfriend there either! I'd simply been doing the same job in the same school for five years, and I felt I needed something new. A friend sent me the advert, and I thought, why not?

Interviewer: What did you find hardest when you first arrived?

Priya: I'd expected the language to be the big problem, but my Spanish actually improved quite quickly. What I found difficult was all the unwritten rules at school. For example, I didn't know how formally I should speak to the head teacher, or whether it was OK to leave the staff room before everyone else. It took me months to feel relaxed.

Interviewer: How are your students different from the ones you taught in England?

Priya: They're not that different, really. Teenagers are teenagers everywhere! But one thing I've noticed is that my students here are much less afraid of making mistakes. They'll just start speaking, even if their English isn't perfect. In England, students often waited until they were sure they were right.

Interviewer: Do teachers there work differently from teachers in the UK?

Priya: In some ways, yes. At first, to be honest, I thought my way of teaching was better. But I've changed my mind. My Chilean colleagues are brilliant at making lessons fun, and I'm probably better at organising things. We've learnt a lot from each other, and I've completely changed some of my lessons because of them.

Interviewer: How do you feel about being so far from your family?

Priya: Honestly, it's been much easier than I feared. We have a video call every Sunday, and my parents have already come to visit twice. The only time I find it really hard is at Christmas, when everyone's together at home and I'm on the other side of the world.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to teachers who are thinking about working abroad?

Priya: Some people say you should learn the language perfectly before you go, but I don't agree. You'll learn it much faster once you're there. My main advice would be to stay for at least two years. In the first year, you're just finding out how everything works. It's only in the second year that you really start to enjoy it.

Interviewer: Priya Shah, thank you very much.

passage.title: The teenager who fixes the city’s bikes
passage.text:
Josh Turner was nineteen when he opened his bicycle repair shop in Leeds. Three years later, the little shop near the canal is busy every day. However, the beginning was not easy.

Josh has loved bikes all his life. His grandfather taught him to mend punctures in the garden shed. “I spent every weekend with oily hands,” he says. At school he was not interested in most subjects, because he preferred taking things apart and putting them back together. After school he started an engineering course at college, but he left after one year. “The course was mostly theory. I wanted to work with real machines,” he explains.

For the next year he repaired bikes for friends and neighbours in his parents’ garage. He charged very little, so soon strangers were knocking on the door with broken bikes. His parents were patient, but the garage was always full. In the end, his mother told him to find a proper workplace.

Josh found an empty shop with a cheap rent, but the problem was money. The banks did not want to lend money to a teenager with no business experience. Finally, his uncle lent him £4,000 for tools and spare parts. Josh promised to pay it all back within two years. He managed it in eighteen months.

The first winter was hard because few people cycle in cold, wet weather, and customers were rare. Some weeks Josh earned almost nothing. He used the quiet time well, though, and built a simple website and started posting short repair videos. In them he shows easy jobs, like adjusting gears or cleaning a chain. Some customers were surprised. “Why do you teach people to fix their own bikes? You’ll lose business!” they said. Josh disagrees. “People watch the videos and try the job at home. Sometimes something goes really wrong. Then they remember my name. They trust me, because I’ve already helped them for free.”

Today Josh employs two part-time mechanics, both students. He also runs a free repair class for local children every Saturday morning. “Lots of kids have bikes with flat tyres in the garage. Nobody shows them how to fix them,” he says.

What advice would he give to other young people? “Don’t wait until you know everything. I made plenty of mistakes in my first year. I ordered the wrong parts, and I forgot to keep receipts. But every mistake taught me something useful.” He smiles. “And find an uncle with some savings!”

passage.title: Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit
passage.text:
Last spring, my partner and I adopted a three-year-old dog called Biscuit from a rescue centre near Leeds. The staff told us that he had spent most of his life alone in a small back garden. (1) ________ For the first two days, he hid behind the sofa and refused to eat anything at all.

In the end, we contacted a local trainer called Megan Hughes. On her first visit, she did not bring any equipment with her. (2) ________ For an hour, she simply sat on the floor with a book and completely ignored Biscuit. By the end of that hour, he was lying next to her feet.

Megan explained that many rescue dogs need time before they can learn anything. (3) ________ So we kept the same routine every day: a walk at seven, breakfast at eight and a quiet hour in the afternoon. After about three weeks, Biscuit started to relax.

Then the real training began. We used tiny pieces of cheese as rewards, and the lessons never lasted more than five minutes. (4) ________ Biscuit learned to sit in a single afternoon, but learning to stay took him much longer.

The hardest part was the park. Other dogs frightened him, and he barked at every bicycle. (5) ________ Now, a year later, he can walk past a busy playground without even looking up. He still hides behind the sofa sometimes, but these days it is usually because he has stolen a sock.

passage.text: When I started college last year, a friend persuaded me to join the student radio station. I had never (1) ______ on the radio before, so I was extremely nervous at my first meeting. Luckily, the station manager, Priya, was very kind. She (2) ______ me to start by reading the weather report, which only (3) ______ about two minutes. Even so, my hands were shaking the first time the red light came on. Little by little, it got easier. After a couple of months I felt (4) ______ enough to ask for my own music programme, and Priya agreed. Now, every Thursday evening from eight to nine, I (5) ______ songs by new bands from our area and chat about them with guests. Some listeners even send messages to request their favourite tracks. Working at the station has (6) ______ me how to plan my time and how to work as part of a team. Next term I am hoping to interview a few local musicians live in the studio, which will be my biggest challenge so far.

passage.title: Five hundred new trees
passage.text: Last autumn our town council asked local people to help plant five hundred young trees along the river path. The project had (1) ______ planned for over a year, but the money only arrived in the summer. On a cold Saturday morning about sixty volunteers met at the old bridge, carrying spades and flasks of hot tea. Very (2) ______ of us had ever planted a tree before, so a gardener from the council showed us what to do. By lunchtime my back was aching, and the work was far (3) ______ tiring than I had expected. Still, it felt good to see the long line of thin trees standing in the grass. The gardener explained that the trees are too young to look after (4) ______ yet. They will not survive their first summer (5) ______ someone waters them regularly. The council has now organised a rota, (6) ______ means that every volunteer spends one evening a month with a watering can. My turn is next Tuesday, and I am already looking forward to it.

passage.text:
Woman: Look, I’ve bought this scarf for my aunt.
Man: It’s lovely. Was it expensive?
Woman: Well, the label said thirty pounds, but there was a sale on, so it was twenty-four. And then the shop assistant noticed a small mark on it and took another six pounds off.
Man: So you paid eighteen pounds? That’s a good price. I can hardly see the mark.

Man: Have you got anything for your brother’s birthday yet? Oliver’s going to be sixteen, isn’t he?
Woman: Yes, and I’ve finally found something. I was going to get him a shirt for his football team, but they didn’t have his size.
Man: What about that board game he keeps talking about?
Woman: Mum’s already bought him that. So in the end I got him some headphones. His old ones are broken.
Man: Good idea. He’ll use them every day.

Man: I’ve decided what to give my mum and dad for their wedding anniversary. I’m taking them out for a meal at that new Italian restaurant.
Woman: How lovely! The anniversary’s on Friday, isn’t it?
Man: Yes, but Dad doesn’t finish work until nine on Fridays. I wanted to go on Saturday evening instead, but the restaurant was fully booked. So we’re going for lunch on Sunday.
Woman: That sounds perfect.

Woman: Good afternoon, shoppers. If you’re looking for that special present, don’t forget our gift-wrapping service on the ground floor. Our normal closing time is half past five, but this week, to help with your Christmas shopping, the store is staying open until seven o’clock. Please note that the gift-wrapping desk closes earlier, at six. Thank you for shopping with us.

Woman: I can’t decide which bag to get for Lucy. This striped one is fun.
Man: Hmm, but she isn’t really a beach person, is she? What about the black backpack? She cycles to work.
Woman: She’s just bought one, actually. No, I think she’d like the brown leather one best. It goes with everything.
Man: It’s more expensive, though.
Woman: That’s fine. She’s my best friend.

Woman: Are you going to Rachel’s leaving party at the office tomorrow?
Man: Yes, and I still haven’t got her anything. I thought about flowers, but they’ll be dead in a week.
Woman: She loves cooking, doesn’t she? What about a recipe book?
Man: She’s got hundreds of those. No, I know. She’s always saying her desk looks empty, so I’ll get her a little plant for her new office.
Woman: Perfect. She’ll love that.

Woman: Granny’s eightieth birthday is next month. What shall we give her?
Man: You’re good at baking. Why don’t you make her a cake?
Woman: Auntie Sue’s already making one. We could make her a birthday card, I suppose.
Man: She’ll get lots of cards. What about putting some old family photos into an album?
Woman: Oh yes, she’d love that. Let’s start looking for photos this weekend.

passage.text:
Woman: Nice watch! Is that one of those smart watches?
Man: Yes. Everyone thinks I got it for my messages, but my phone’s fine for that.
Woman: So is it for running?
Man: Not really. The doctor said I wasn’t sleeping enough, so I wanted to know how many hours I really get each night. The watch shows me every morning. It’s already made me go to bed earlier.
Woman: And it looks good too.
Man: That’s just a bonus.

Woman: Are you still using that running app?
Man: Every day! I know it isn’t free, and it took me a few days to understand all the buttons, but now it’s easy. Honestly, without it I’d have stopped running weeks ago. When it tells me I’ve beaten my best time, I just want to go out again the next morning.
Woman: Maybe I should try it, then.
Man: You should. It’s worth every penny.

Man: How are you getting on with the new booking system?
Woman: Not very well! I’m sure it’s better than the old one, but nobody showed us how it works.
Man: Exactly. We had one short email from the manager and that was it. They should have given us a proper course before it started.
Woman: I agree. I spent half the morning asking people for help.
Man: Me too. Maybe it’ll save us time when we know what we’re doing, but I’m not so sure.

Man: So did your family really spend a whole evening without phones?
Woman: We did. To be honest, I thought I’d hate it. I thought I’d keep worrying about missing messages.
Man: And did you?
Woman: For about ten minutes! Then we got a board game out and laughed all evening. My kids didn’t even ask for their phones. We’re going to do it every Friday now.

Woman: I had my first video call with Grandma and Grandad last night.
Man: How did it go? I bet it took ages to get them connected.
Woman: That’s what I expected! I was ready to spend an hour explaining which buttons to press. But Grandad had practised with a neighbour, and it worked first time. We chatted for ages, and I could hear them perfectly.
Man: That’s brilliant.
Woman: Honestly, it was the best part of my week.

Man: Are you still learning Spanish with that app?
Woman: No, I gave up last month.
Man: Really? I thought it was free.
Woman: It is, and the games were fun. I learned loads of words. But when I went to Valencia, I couldn’t have a single conversation with anyone. All I’d done was press buttons! So now I go to an evening class where we actually talk to each other.
Man: That sounds much more useful.

passage.text:
Woman: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsley Theatre. My name’s Helen and I’ll be your guide this morning. The tour takes about an hour, so I hope you’re all wearing comfortable shoes.

Let’s start with a bit of history. A lot of visitors think this building was once a church, because of the tall windows, but in fact it was built as a fish market. It only became a theatre in 1904, when a local businessman bought it and turned it into the place you see today.

Now, if you follow me into the main hall… Here we are. When the theatre first opened, it had space for twelve hundred people, but in those days the seats were very narrow. After we put in new, more comfortable seats ten years ago, the number went down, and today we have eight hundred and fifty seats.

Do look up at the ceiling. People usually expect a theatre ceiling to be red, but ours is green, with little gold stars painted all over it. It was cleaned last spring, so the colours are really bright again.

Next we’re going backstage. Down these stairs is the workshop where the costumes are made. We have a team of four people who make everything by hand. The wigs, by the way, aren’t made here. We order those from a company in London.

Right, now we’re on the stage itself. You’re welcome to walk around, and you can even sit on the furniture, which is from tonight’s show. The only thing I must ask is that you don’t touch the ropes at the side of the stage. They hold up the scenery, and they’re very heavy.

That’s nearly the end of the tour. Before you go, keep hold of your ticket. If you show it in the café on the ground floor, you’ll get ten per cent off anything you buy there today. I’m afraid the discount doesn’t work in the gift shop, though. Thank you all for coming, and I hope you enjoy the rest of your day.

Woman: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsley Theatre. My name’s Helen and I’ll be your guide this morning. The tour takes about an hour, so I hope you’re all wearing comfortable shoes.

Let’s start with a bit of history. A lot of visitors think this building was once a church, because of the tall windows, but in fact it was built as a fish market. It only became a theatre in 1904, when a local businessman bought it and turned it into the place you see today.

Now, if you follow me into the main hall… Here we are. When the theatre first opened, it had space for twelve hundred people, but in those days the seats were very narrow. After we put in new, more comfortable seats ten years ago, the number went down, and today we have eight hundred and fifty seats.

Do look up at the ceiling. People usually expect a theatre ceiling to be red, but ours is green, with little gold stars painted all over it. It was cleaned last spring, so the colours are really bright again.

Next we’re going backstage. Down these stairs is the workshop where the costumes are made. We have a team of four people who make everything by hand. The wigs, by the way, aren’t made here. We order those from a company in London.

Right, now we’re on the stage itself. You’re welcome to walk around, and you can even sit on the furniture, which is from tonight’s show. The only thing I must ask is that you don’t touch the ropes at the side of the stage. They hold up the scenery, and they’re very heavy.

That’s nearly the end of the tour. Before you go, keep hold of your ticket. If you show it in the café on the ground floor, you’ll get ten per cent off anything you buy there today. I’m afraid the discount doesn’t work in the gift shop, though. Thank you all for coming, and I hope you enjoy the rest of your day.

passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking to Megan Price, who opened her own bakery in the town of Ludlow two years ago. Megan, you used to work in an office, didn’t you?

Megan: That’s right, I was in a bank for six years. The pay was fine and my colleagues were lovely, so people were surprised when I left. But I’d been baking at weekends for years, and I realised that Saturday mornings in the kitchen were the only time I felt really happy. In the end, I just couldn’t keep doing a job I didn’t care about.

Interviewer: How did you feel on the day the shop opened?

Megan: Honestly, I was terrified. Not about the baking, because I knew my bread was good. I kept thinking: what if I’ve spent all my savings and nobody comes through the door? Then at half past seven there was a queue outside, and I nearly cried.

Interviewer: Bakers start work very early. How do you cope with that?

Megan: I start at four. Everyone warned me it would be awful, but actually I don’t mind it at all. The streets are quiet, the radio’s on, and I get more done in those two hours than I used to in a whole day at the bank. What I do find hard is going to bed at nine.

Interviewer: What makes a good bakery, in your opinion?

Megan: Lots of people would say the recipes, and of course they matter. But for me, it’s the people behind the counter. If customers feel welcome, if you remember their names and what they like, they’ll come back even on a day when the croissants aren’t perfect.

Interviewer: A lot of people buy their bread in supermarkets. Does that worry you?

Megan: Not really. Some supermarket bread is perfectly nice, and it’s cheaper than mine, I know that. But I don’t think we’re really competing. People come to me for a treat, or for something special at the weekend, not for their everyday sandwich loaf.

Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who’d like to start their own business?

Megan: Don’t wait until everything is perfect, because it never will be. But do get some experience first. I worked in another baker’s shop on Saturdays for a year before I opened mine, and I learned more there than from any book.

Interviewer: Megan Price, thank you very much.

passage.title: On her toes: an interview with Isla Mackenzie
passage.text:
Isla Mackenzie is seventeen and comes from Glasgow, and last month she won a place at a famous dance school in London. We asked her about her life so far.

When did you start dancing?
I started when I was six. My older sister went to ballet classes, and I had to wait for her every Saturday until her class finished. I watched through the window and copied all the steps that the older girls did. One day the teacher noticed me and invited me in. My sister stopped after a year, but I never did.

Was ballet always your favourite?
No, it wasn’t at first. To be honest, I found it quite boring as a child because there were so many rules. Then, when I was eleven, I tried contemporary dance, which felt much freer. Suddenly I understood the point of ballet. It gives you strength and control. Now I do both styles.

How much do you train?
About twenty hours a week. I go to school as normal, and then I dance every evening and on Saturdays as well. My friends often go to the cinema while I’m training. That used to upset me, but now I accept it. I see them on Sundays, and they come to all my shows.

Have you ever wanted to give up?
Only once, when I was fourteen. I hurt my ankle badly and couldn’t dance for four months. I felt completely lost because dancing was my whole life. My physiotherapist gave me exercises that I did every day. During that time I started to watch other dancers more carefully. I noticed small details in their movements. Strangely, I came back a better dancer.

How did the audition for the London school go when you finally went there?
I was terribly nervous because there were three hundred people for only thirty places. First we did a ballet class, and then we each performed a short piece. I chose a contemporary piece by my own teacher. In the middle I slipped slightly, but I didn’t stop. I just carried on and smiled. Afterwards one of the judges told me that she liked that moment the most. In her opinion, it showed my character.

What are you worried about?
Moving away from home, mostly, because I’ve never lived alone, and I can’t cook at all! My mum is giving me lessons this summer so that I don’t starve. London is expensive too, so money is a bit of a worry. Luckily, I’ve got a grant that pays for the fees.

What would you say to young people who want to dance?
Dance because you love it, not for fame. Most dancers never become stars, and that’s fine. The joy is in the dancing itself.

passage.title: From the sofa to the finish line
passage.text:
Two years ago, Owen Price could not run for a bus. The 45-year-old taxi driver from Cardiff spent most of his day sitting down, and he hardly ever did any exercise. (1) ________ His doctor told him that his blood pressure was too high and that he needed to become more active.

Owen decided to start with something small. He downloaded a free app that mixed one minute of running with ninety seconds of walking. (2) ________ After nine weeks, however, he could run for thirty minutes without stopping, and he felt prouder than he had felt for years.

That was when his daughter, Carys, suggested a marathon. Owen laughed at first. (3) ________ However, Carys had already found a six-month training plan for beginners. It started with three short runs a week and slowly added longer runs at weekends.

The plan was not always easy to follow. In January, the weather was terrible and Owen caught a bad cold. (4) ________ Instead of giving up, he went back to shorter runs for a fortnight until he felt strong again.

On race day, the crowds along the streets were enormous. Owen remembered the advice from Carys and started slowly. (5) ________ He finished in five hours and twelve minutes, and Carys was waiting at the finish line with a cup of tea. Now he wants to run the race again next year and beat his own time.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
passage.text:
Man: So which animal are you going to photograph for the competition?
Woman: Everyone will take pictures of the lions, so I don’t want to do that. I thought about the penguins, but they’re inside, behind glass, and you get terrible reflections.
Man: What about the giraffes? They’re outside, and the light’s lovely there in the afternoon.
Woman: Yes, they’re the ones. I’ll go over there after lunch.

Man: You’re back early from your walk.
Woman: It started raining. But guess what I saw by the river? A deer! It was just standing there, drinking.
Man: Really? I’ve only ever seen foxes round here.
Woman: I usually see rabbits in the field next to the river, but there weren’t any today. The deer ran off as soon as it heard me.

Woman: Well, I’ve checked Max all over. He’s healthy, but he’s a bit heavy for a dog of his size.
Man: Oh dear. Should I change his food, or give him less?
Woman: No, his food is fine, and he’s eating the right amount. The problem is exercise. How long are his walks?
Man: About fifteen minutes, twice a day.
Woman: That isn’t enough for a young dog like Max. Try to make each walk at least forty minutes, and bring him back to see me in a month.

Man: I’ve started volunteering at the animal centre on Saturdays.
Woman: Really? What do you do there? Clean the cages?
Man: Most volunteers do that, but they’ve got enough people for it now. Last week I fed the rabbits, but this Saturday they’ve asked me to take some of the dogs out for walks.
Woman: That sounds like the best job of all.

Woman: Welcome to Hill Farm, boys and girls. Now, I know you all want to ride the ponies, but they’re having a rest at the moment, so we’ll do that at two o’clock. The baby lambs are asleep in the barn, so we’ll visit them after the ponies. So let’s start by giving the goats some food. Take a bag each from the box by the gate, and follow me.

Woman: Have you seen Tiger? I’ve looked under the bed and in all the cupboards.
Man: He was on the garage roof earlier, sitting in the sun.
Woman: He isn’t there now. I’ve just looked.
Man: Wait, listen. Can you hear that? It’s coming from inside the garage. I left the door open when I got the bikes out. He must have gone in there.
Woman: Oh yes, there he is, next to the bikes. Silly cat!

Woman: Did you hear? Our dog Bella had her puppies last night.
Man: Oh, that’s exciting! How many?
Woman: The vet thought there would be eight, but in the end there were five.
Man: Are you going to keep them all?
Woman: No way! Six people have already asked us for one, so finding homes for them won’t be a problem.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
passage.text:
Man: Have you been to the new café where the bookshop used to be?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. I was sad when the bookshop closed, I must admit. But the café’s lovely. They’ve kept some of the old shelves, and there are books you can borrow while you have your coffee.
Man: Isn’t it expensive, though?
Woman: A bit more than the place by the station, but I don’t mind. It feels like the bookshop never really left.

Woman: Are you going to the meeting at the library tonight?
Man: Yes. I expect most people will complain about parking.
Woman: It’s the building work that bothers me. It’s so noisy.
Man: That’ll be finished in a month. No, I’m going because they want to turn the empty land behind the school into a playground, and some people are against it. My kids have got nowhere to play round here, so I want to speak up for it.
Woman: Good for you.

Woman: Did you read in the local paper that the council wants to close Mill Road to cars on Sunday mornings?
Man: I did. The idea is that children can play in the street.
Woman: I’m not sure many children would use it, actually. And the shopkeepers are worried they’ll lose customers.
Man: I think they’ll get more people walking past. But the council should ask the people who live here before it decides anything.
Woman: Absolutely. Nobody’s asked us a thing.

Woman: Did you see in the paper that the Regal Cinema is going to be turned into flats?
Man: Yes. It’s sad. I saw my first film there.
Woman: Lots of people are saying the council should repair it and open it again.
Man: I’d love that, but who would go? It’s been closed for eight years, and everyone watches films at the big cinema by the shopping centre now. Young people round here can’t find anywhere to live, so flats make sense.
Woman: I suppose you’re right.

Man: How was the street party in the end?
Woman: Well, it was hard work. Weeks of letters, phone calls, borrowing tables. I nearly gave up twice.
Man: Was it expensive?
Woman: No, the council lent us the tables for free, so it hardly cost anything. And on the day about sixty people came. I talked to neighbours I’d never spoken to in ten years of living there.
Man: So will you do it again next year?
Woman: Definitely. I’m really glad I did it.

Man: How’s the new flat in Ashford Street?
Woman: I love it. I was worried because it’s near the main road, but my bedroom’s at the back, so I hardly hear the traffic.
Man: And the neighbours?
Woman: That’s the best thing. The day I moved in, the woman next door brought me a cake, and the man upstairs helped me carry my sofa. In my old street nobody even said hello.
Man: Is it far from work?
Woman: Twenty minutes on the bus. About the same as before.

passage.text:
Man: And now some exciting news for all you young writers out there. Here at Radio Harbourside we’re running our Young Writers’ Competition again, and this year it’s bigger than ever.

First of all, who can enter? Last year the competition was open to anyone between eleven and eighteen, but we had so many entries from older teenagers that this year we’re making it just for younger writers. So, if you’re aged between eleven and sixteen, you can take part.

Now, the subject. Last year’s stories were all about friendship, and we read some wonderful ones. This year we want you to write a story about a journey. It could be a trip to the other side of the world or just the walk to school. Use your imagination!

Your story mustn’t be longer than eight hundred words. I know some competitions ask for five hundred, but we want to give you a bit more space. Please don’t go over the limit, though, or the judges won’t read it.

Here’s the really exciting part. The three best stories will be read out on the radio in June. Not by me, I’m pleased to say, but by a well-known actor. We can’t tell you who yet, but you’ll certainly recognise the voice.

And the prizes? Everyone on the shortlist gets a set of books, and the winner will receive a laptop, which we hope will help with all your future writing.

To enter, just send your story to the address on our website before the thirtieth of April. Don’t forget to put your name and age at the top. We won’t be sending emails to tell people the results. Instead, the winners will be contacted by phone in the middle of May, so make sure you include a phone number for a parent or carer.

Good luck, everybody. We can’t wait to read your stories.

passage.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Aisha Bello, who’s just twenty-three and runs her own recycling business in Leeds. Aisha, tell us what you do.

Aisha: We collect old jeans from charity shops, from people’s wardrobes, from anywhere really, and turn them into bags, cushions and pencil cases. Last year we saved about four tonnes of denim from going to the rubbish tip.

Interviewer: How did the idea start?

Aisha: At university I shared a flat with three other students, and when we moved out, the amount of clothing we threw away shocked me. I’d always thought of myself as someone who cared about the environment, and suddenly I felt quite ashamed. That’s really what got me started. Making money didn’t come into it at first.

Interviewer: Was it difficult to get going?

Aisha: The sewing wasn’t a problem. My grandmother taught me when I was small. The hard part was persuading shops to stock our products. Some of them said recycled things looked cheap. I had to keep going back with better and better samples, and eventually one shop in York said yes.

Interviewer: You now have six people working for you. What’s that like?

Aisha: I love it, although being a boss was a big change. At first I tried to check everything myself, and I was exhausted. Now I trust the team to make their own decisions, and honestly, they often have better ideas than I do.

Interviewer: Your bags aren’t cheap, are they?

Aisha: No, and I won’t pretend they are. Every one is made by hand here in Leeds, and we pay our staff properly. Some customers do complain, but most of them understand that if you want something made fairly, it’s going to cost a bit more.

Interviewer: Some people say small recycling businesses can’t really make a difference. What do you think?

Aisha: I understand why they say it. One small company won’t save the planet. But I think we do something important by showing people that old things can be beautiful. When customers see what we make, they start looking at their own clothes differently, and that matters more than the tonnes we collect.

Interviewer: And what’s next for you?

Aisha: People keep telling me to open a big factory, but I’m not interested in growing too fast. I’d rather stay small and do things properly. What I would like is to run workshops in schools, so that children can learn to repair their own clothes.

Interviewer: Aisha Bello, thanks for talking to us.
