passage.title: The kitchen scientist
passage.text:
Every Sunday afternoon, sixteen-year-old Priya Shah turns her family’s kitchen in Cardiff into a science laboratory. She puts her phone on a pile of books and starts filming while her parents are out. Her short videos explain everyday science, such as the reason bread rises or ice floats. Her channel, Kitchen Lab, now has more than 80,000 subscribers.

Priya never planned to become a video maker. Two years ago she was having problems with chemistry at school. Her textbook seemed dull, and the diagrams meant nothing to her. One evening she tried an experiment from the book at home, with vinegar and baking soda. Suddenly the reaction made sense. Her cousin was having the same problem with chemistry, so she filmed the next experiment for him. He shared it with his class, and soon strangers were asking for more.

The first videos were not very good because the sound was poor, and Priya talked too fast. Some viewers left unkind comments. “I nearly deleted everything after the first month,” she admits. Her older brother persuaded her to continue. He bought her a cheap microphone and showed her how to edit. Now each video takes about six hours to make. Most of that time goes on research. “I check every fact in at least two places. A mistake in a science video is worse than no video at all.”

Safety is important to her too, so she never uses dangerous chemicals. Every experiment uses things from an ordinary kitchen. At the start of each video, she reminds younger viewers to ask an adult for help.

Her chemistry teacher, Mr Evans, is a big fan who sometimes shows her videos in his lessons. “Priya explains things in the language of teenagers,” he says. “Students listen to her in a different way. They listen to me because they have to!”

Success has brought some surprises. Last spring a university invited her to speak at a science festival. She was terrified of the large audience, but she enjoyed it in the end. Companies have also offered her money to advertise their products. So far she has said no to all of them. “My viewers trust me. I don’t want them to think I’m selling something.”

Priya wants to study medicine, so she is not sure about the future of Kitchen Lab. “Maybe I’ll stop, maybe I won’t. For now, it’s fun, and I’m learning more than my viewers!”

passage.title: Six pupils and one teacher
passage.text:
On the island of Inchmara, off the west coast of Scotland, there is a primary school with just six pupils. They are between five and eleven years old, and they all learn together in one classroom. (1) ________ Fiona MacLeod has worked at the school for nine years, and she says that she would never change her job.

Teaching children of such different ages is not simple. Every morning, Fiona gives each pupil a plan for the day. (2) ________ The older ones often help the younger ones with their reading, and this is good for both groups.

The island has no shops apart from a small post office, and the ferry to the mainland only sails three times a week. (3) ________ Instead, the children use the island itself as a classroom. In science lessons, they study the birds on the cliffs, and in maths they measure the height of the waves.

Some people worry that the children do not have enough friends of their own age. (4) ________ Twice a term, the pupils take the ferry to a larger school on the mainland and spend the day with children of the same age. They also have a video call every week with a small school in Norway.

The biggest problem for the school is its future. Two of the pupils will leave for secondary school next summer, and only one new child is expected. (5) ________ But Fiona is hopeful. Several young families have moved to the island recently, because they can now work from home online.

passage.text: Last month my father turned fifty, and I offered to cook a special dinner for the whole family. I had watched lots of cooking programmes, so I was sure it would be easy. passage.text:
Woman: Hello, I’m calling about my laptop. You were going to look at the keyboard.
Man: Yes. I’m afraid we can’t repair it, so we’ll need to put a new one in. Normally that’s seventy-five pounds altogether, sixty for the keyboard and fifteen for the work. But because you bought the laptop here, we won’t charge for the work.
Woman: So it’ll be sixty pounds?
Man: Less than that, actually. There’s fifteen pounds off all keyboards this month, so it’s just forty-five.
Woman: Great. Please go ahead.

Man: How was your computer course?
Woman: Really good. I wanted to learn how to make a website for my business, but that course was full, so I did the one on photos instead. Now I can make all my holiday pictures look professional.
Man: Maybe you could do the website course next term.
Woman: Yes, I will. My son also wants me to try making computer games with him, but I don’t think so!

Man: So which one are you going to get?
Woman: I really liked the small laptop, but the screen’s too small for my design work.
Man: And the tablet with the keyboard? You could take it anywhere.
Woman: I don’t need to take it anywhere. I always work at home. So I’m going for the desktop computer. It’s got a huge screen, and it’s cheaper too.

Woman: Have you found your tablet?
Man: Yes, thank goodness. I was sure I’d left it on the bus, so I phoned the bus company, but they didn’t have it. Then I remembered I’d used it in the café after I left the library.
Woman: And it was there?
Man: Yes. The waiter had kept it behind the counter for me.

Man: Is that a new phone case?
Woman: Yes. I dropped my phone last week, so I thought I’d better protect it. Luckily the screen didn’t break, and the battery’s fine too. The only problem is that the camera doesn’t work any more, and I need it for my photography course.
Man: You should take it to the repair shop on Market Street. They’re really quick.

Man: Excuse me, do you sell chargers for this phone?
Woman: Yes, they’re over there, next to the phone cases.
Man: Great. I left mine at my hotel. Oh, and have you got any earphones?
Woman: Sorry, we’ve sold out. We’ll have more on Friday.
Man: Never mind. I’ll just take the charger, then.

Woman: Hello, this is Sarah from Fastline Broadband with a message for Mr Patel. You booked an engineer to look at your internet connection tomorrow at nine o’clock. I’m afraid he’s ill, so another engineer will come instead. She’s busy until half past eleven, so she can’t come in the morning, but she’ll be with you at two o’clock. Please call us back if that time is a problem.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
passage.text:
Woman: Did you get the letter from the school about plastic bottles?
Man: Yes. From next month the children have to bring metal ones instead.
Woman: I think it’s a good idea, but the school should give them one each. Not every family can pay fifteen pounds for a bottle.
Man: You’re right. That’s the real problem.
Woman: Mind you, my son Leo will probably lose his in a week.
Man: Oh, I don’t think so. My daughter’s had the same lunch box for three years.

Woman: You’re going to Edinburgh by train? From Cornwall? That’s nine hours!
Man: I know. And it cost more than the plane, too.
Woman: So why? Are you scared of flying?
Man: No, I fly for work all the time. But I read how much pollution one flight makes, and I felt terrible. This time I wanted to travel in a way that’s better for the planet. And I’ll get lots of reading done.

Man: How was the beach clean-up on Saturday?
Woman: Really well organised. They gave us gloves and bags, and there were about forty of us. But what shocked me was how much of the rubbish was plastic packaging, exactly like the stuff I buy every week.
Man: Really?
Woman: Since then I’ve been taking my own containers to the market and buying fruit without any packaging. I’ll never look at a supermarket shelf in the same way again.

Woman: Do you really cycle to work every day now?
Man: Since March. I only started because my car broke down and I didn’t want to pay for the repair straight away.
Woman: Isn’t it dangerous on the main road?
Man: There’s a cycle path most of the way, so I feel quite safe. And it’s only five minutes slower than driving, with all the traffic. The funny thing is, I actually look forward to it now. I never thought I’d say that!

Man: That’s a great jacket. Is it new?
Woman: No, it’s second-hand, from the charity shop on Church Street.
Man: Really? You love that seventies look, don’t you?
Woman: Not especially. This one just fitted me. I used to buy new clothes all the time, but then I watched a programme about how many clothes get thrown away every year. Millions of tonnes! So now I try not to buy anything new.
Man: It must save you money too.
Woman: Not always. Some of those shops aren’t cheap. But that isn’t why I do it.

Man: Have you seen the little brown bin the council left for food waste?
Woman: Yes, and I was ready to hate it. I thought the whole kitchen would smell.
Man: And does it?
Woman: Not at all. The lid closes really tightly. And our ordinary bin’s half empty now, so we only take the rubbish out once a week. Honestly, it’s made life easier.
Man: Hmm. I’m still not sure it’s worth all the trouble.

passage.text:
Woman: Hi everyone, I’m Ruth, and I’m organising this year’s River Wendle Clean-Up Day, which is happening on Sunday the fourteenth of May. Thanks for coming to this meeting. Let me tell you what you need to know.

We’ll all meet in the car park next to the old mill, at the bottom of Station Road. Please don’t go to the bridge in the town centre. That’s where we met last year, but there’s building work there at the moment.

The poster says we’re starting at ten o’clock, but that was a mistake, I’m afraid. We’ll actually start at half past nine, so please try to arrive a few minutes before that.

As for equipment, we’ll give everyone rubbish bags and litter pickers, those long grabbers, so you won’t need to bring those. What you do need to bring is a pair of gloves. Strong ones, please, because there can be broken glass near the water. And wear old clothes, as you’re going to get muddy.

You might be wondering what we find. Mostly it’s plastic bottles and cans, of course, and every year there are a couple of shopping trolleys. But the strangest thing we pulled out last year was a guitar. It was in surprisingly good condition, actually!

At about one o’clock we’ll stop for lunch. The café by the river has closed down, unfortunately, but a local bakery has kindly offered to bring sandwiches and cakes for everyone, free of charge.

Finally, families are very welcome. Children aged fourteen and over can come on their own, but anyone under fourteen must be with an adult. Last year the age was twelve, but we’ve changed it because some parts of the riverbank are quite steep.

If you have any questions, you can find me after the meeting. See you on the fourteenth!

passage.text:
Interviewer: I’m here with seventeen-year-old Leo Hartley, who has just been chosen for the national youth climbing team. Leo, how did you get into climbing?

Leo: It was because of my older sister, really. She went to a climbing wall for a friend’s birthday party and loved it, and the next week I went along with her, just because I was bored. I wasn’t sporty at all. I was terrible at football, so I didn’t expect much. But after ten minutes on the wall I knew I’d found my thing.

Interviewer: What is it about climbing that you enjoy most?

Leo: People think it’s all about being strong, and you do need strength. But for me the best part is the puzzle. Every route is different, and you have to work out where to put your hands and feet. When you finally manage a route you’ve been stuck on for weeks, it’s an amazing feeling.

Interviewer: Do you prefer climbing indoors or outdoors?

Leo: Competitions are all indoors, so I train on climbing walls most of the time, and they’re great for practising. But nothing compares to being on real rock in the mountains. The views, the quiet… Whenever I can, I go to Wales with my coach.

Interviewer: Is climbing dangerous?

Leo: Everyone asks that! My mum worried a lot at first. But honestly, with the right equipment and a good partner, it’s much safer than most people imagine. Accidents usually happen when people get careless, so I always check everything twice.

Interviewer: How do you manage school and training?

Leo: It isn’t easy. I train five evenings a week, so I do my homework on the bus and at lunchtime. My teachers have been really understanding, though. When I had a competition in France, they sent me work to do so that I didn’t fall behind.

Interviewer: What are your hopes for the future?

Leo: Lots of people expect me to say the Olympics. That would be incredible, of course, but I try not to think that far ahead. Right now I just want to keep enjoying it. If I stop having fun, there’s no point.

Interviewer: Leo, good luck.

passage.title: 312 bottles: how our school changed
passage.text:
Amara Okafor, fifteen, explains how her school cut its plastic waste.

Last year I counted the plastic bottles in the bins at my school in Plymouth. It took me a whole lunch break. In one day there were 312 bottles, and almost none of them were recycled. That number shocked me so much that it became the start of our project.

At first I tried to do everything alone. I put a cardboard box in the canteen with a sign: “Bottles here, please”. After a week the box was full of crisp packets, apple cores and chewing gum. I felt like giving up. My form tutor, Ms Hughes, had a different idea. “People don’t change because of a box,” she told me. “They change because their friends do.”

So I asked for volunteers. Six students from different year groups joined me, and we called ourselves the Green Team. Each of us talked to our own class about what we had found. We also made a short film about the bottles and showed it in assembly. The younger students loved it, but some older ones laughed at us. That was hard. For a few days I felt quite embarrassed in the corridors.

Next we needed proper recycling bins. The head teacher liked the idea, but there was no money for them. We organised a cake sale and a sponsored walk along the coast. Together they raised £650, enough for ten bins. A local company that collects rubbish agreed to empty them for free every week.

The bins helped, but the biggest change came from the water fountains. Two fountains in the school had been broken for months. We wrote a letter to the head teacher, and they were repaired. We also sold metal water bottles with the school badge on them. Now most students fill up their own bottle. They no longer buy a new one every day.

This year we counted again. On an average day there are fewer than forty plastic bottles, and nearly all of them go into the recycling bins. Other schools in the city have asked us for advice. In May we even gave a talk at a meeting for local teachers.

People often ask me about the lessons of the project. For me, the people are more important than the numbers. A project like this needs a team. I am quite shy, and I could never speak in assembly on my own. Working with others gave me confidence. Next year I want to start on food waste. It will be harder, but I am not worried because our team is bigger now.

questions.question: What did Ms Hughes think about the cardboard box?
options: a) It would not change habits on its own.
b) It just needed a little more time.
c) It needed a clearer sign on it.
d) It should be in a different place.

questions.question: What does Amara say was difficult about the film in assembly?
options: a) The younger students did not understand it.
b) Some older students made fun of the team.
c) Nobody wanted to join the team after seeing it.
d) It took the team a very long time to make.

questions.question: How did the school get its recycling bins?
options: a) The head teacher paid for them from the school budget.
b) A local company gave them to the school for free.
c) The city council sent them after a letter from the team.

passage.title: The Cornish pasty: a lunch with a handle
passage.text:
Today you can buy a Cornish pasty at almost any railway station in Britain, but this famous snack began as a working lunch. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, thousands of men worked in the tin and copper mines of Cornwall, in the far south-west of England. (1) ________ They needed a meal that was filling, easy to carry and still warm several hours later.

The pasty was the perfect answer. It is made from a circle of pastry, folded over a filling of beef, potato, onion and a vegetable called swede. (2) ________ According to a popular story, the miners held the pasty by this thick edge, because their hands were often dirty. They ate the rest and threw the crust away.

Some families had their own special recipes, and some pasties even had meat at one end and fruit at the other. (3) ________ That way, each man knew which pasty was his, even when they were all kept warm together.

When the mines started to close in the late nineteenth century, many Cornish miners moved abroad to find work. (4) ________ As a result, you can still find pasties today in parts of Mexico, Australia and the United States.

In 2011, the Cornish pasty received special protection from the European Union. (5) ________ It must also have the famous D shape, with the crimp on one side. For the people of Cornwall, this was an important way to protect a piece of their history.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
passage.text:
Man: I heard you’ve left the hospital.
Woman: Yes. After eight years as a nurse, I wanted a change. I thought about teaching, but you need another year of training for that.
Man: So what are you doing now?
Woman: I’m working on reception at the Park Hotel. I love meeting people from all over the world.

Man: So, we’ll see you on Monday at nine. Have you got everything you need?
Woman: I think so. Do I need to bring my passport?
Man: No, we saw that at the interview. And we’ll take your photo for your ID card here. But we haven’t got your bank details yet, so please bring those, or we can’t pay you!
Woman: Of course. I’ll bring them with me.

Woman: Good morning, Tom. I know you usually start by checking the emails, but can you leave them until later today? The delivery’s coming at ten, and the storeroom’s in a terrible mess. Could you sort that out first?
Man: Of course. And what about Mrs Green? She wanted someone to call her back.
Woman: Don’t worry, I’ll phone her myself.

Man: Is the team meeting still in Meeting Room Two this afternoon?
Woman: No, there’s a problem with the heating in there. It’s freezing.
Man: We could go to the café downstairs.
Woman: It’s too noisy. Let’s use the staff kitchen. There’s a big table, and nobody uses it after lunch.
Man: OK, I’ll tell everyone.

Man: What’s it like working at the park?
Woman: It’s great. In summer I spend most of the day cutting the grass, which gets a bit boring. Sometimes visitors stop and ask me questions, and that’s nice. But the best part is in autumn, when we plant new trees. It’s hard work, but I know they’ll still be there in a hundred years.

Woman: Hi, are you the engineer? The printer on this floor isn’t working.
Man: Actually, I’m here for the photocopier. Your office manager called us this morning.
Woman: Oh, the photocopier? I didn’t know that was broken too.
Man: Yes, it’s making a strange noise, apparently. I’m afraid I don’t do printers. You’ll need to call a different company for that.
Woman: And I don’t suppose you can do anything about the coffee machine either!

Woman: Are you on the afternoon shift again next week, Dan?
Man: No. I’ve been doing two o’clock starts for a month now, so they’ve moved me. Next week I’m on the early shift.
Woman: Eight o’clock? That’s not too bad.
Man: I wish! The early shift starts at six now. I’ll have to get up at five.

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
passage.text:
Woman: Every Saturday at the dog shelter? That’s kind of you.
Man: It isn’t that kind, really. I’ve always wanted a dog, but pets aren’t allowed in my flat. This way I get to spend time with dogs without breaking the rules.
Woman: And you must get fit, walking all those dogs.
Man: I already run every day, so that’s not the point.
Woman: Have you ever thought of working with animals?
Man: Not seriously. I’m happy in my job.

Man: I thought you wanted a kitten.
Woman: So did I! The rescue centre had lots of them. But the staff told me kittens are full of energy and climb all over the furniture. I work from home, and I need peace and quiet for that. Biscuit’s nine, and she just sleeps on the chair next to my desk all day.
Man: Was she cheaper than a kitten?
Woman: No, it was the same price, actually.

Woman: Did you watch that programme about foxes last night?
Man: I did. I used to think foxes were just a nuisance. One keeps opening our bins.
Woman: Me too.
Man: But I feel differently now. It showed how clever they are, and how hard it is for them to raise their cubs in a city. There was one sad bit when a cub got lost, but it found its mother in the end.
Woman: I fell asleep before the end. It was an hour and a half!
Man: I didn’t notice the time at all.

Woman: Well, what did you think of the wildlife park?
Man: The animals looked healthy, and they had loads of space. Not like the old zoo in town.
Woman: True. The keepers obviously care about them. But the café was a disaster. Twenty minutes for a sandwich!
Man: I didn’t mind that. What I didn’t like was the price. Thirty pounds each is too much.
Woman: Hmm, for a whole day out, I think it’s fair.

Woman: How are the training classes going with Rocky?
Man: Better than I hoped. I thought the trainer would just teach Rocky to sit, but really she teaches the owners. Most of the problems were my fault. I was giving him treats at the wrong time!
Woman: Aren’t those classes expensive?
Man: Twenty pounds each, but they’re worth it. And Rocky’s only one, so he learns fast.

Man: How’s your daughter’s rabbit?
Woman: Well, she begged for him for a year and promised she’d look after him. For the first month she did. Now guess who cleans the cage every Sunday?
Man: You?
Woman: Me! But the strange thing is, I don’t mind at all. I sit with him in the garden in the evenings, and he’s really become my rabbit too. I’m quite glad she wanted one.

Man: Good afternoon. I’m David Moss, manager of the new Westgate Shopping Centre, and I’d like to tell you about our opening day this Saturday.

The doors will open at nine o’clock, and at ten the centre will be officially opened by a well-known footballer who grew up here in Northfield. There were stories in the local paper that a famous singer was coming, but I’m afraid that isn’t true.

So, what will you find inside? On Saturday there will be sixty-five shops open, on three floors. We had hoped to have seventy by the opening day, but a few aren’t quite ready yet, so those will open later in the year.

On the top floor there’s a cinema with six screens, and next to it a food court with restaurants from all over the world. We’re also planning a bowling alley, but that won’t be finished until next summer.

Getting here is easy. Our car park has space for a thousand cars, and parking is free for the first two hours. After that it costs one pound an hour. If you’d rather leave the car at home, the number forty-two bus stops right outside the main entrance. The number twenty-four also comes to this part of town, but it stops on the other side of the river, which is quite a long walk.

And finally, a little gift. Lots of new shopping centres give away shopping bags on their opening day, but we thought we’d do something different. So the first hundred customers through the door will each get a free umbrella, in our special Westgate colours. Very useful in this weather!

We’re really looking forward to seeing you all on Saturday.

passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking to Jess Moran, who’s nineteen and plays the drums in the band Paper Lanterns. Their first album came out last month. Jess, how did the band start?

Jess: We all met at college in Brighton. Sam, our singer, put a note on the noticeboard asking for a drummer, and I almost didn’t reply, because I didn’t think I was good enough. My best friend made me go to the first practice. I’m so glad she did.

Interviewer: What was it like recording your first album?

Jess: Harder than I expected. On stage, if you make a small mistake, nobody notices because everyone’s dancing. In the studio, you have to play the same song again and again until it’s perfect. Some days I got really fed up. But it taught me a lot about being patient.

Interviewer: Do you all agree about the kind of music you want to make?

Jess: Not at all! We argue about it all the time. Sam likes slow, sad songs and I prefer something you can dance to. But actually, I think that’s why our music works. If we all wanted the same thing, it would be boring.

Interviewer: Lots of bands become famous online these days. How do you feel about social media?

Jess: It’s useful, I can’t deny that. Most of our fans found us through videos online. But I don’t enjoy it. I’d much rather spend my time writing music than thinking about what to post every day. Luckily, our bass player loves doing it.

Interviewer: What’s your favourite thing about being in a band?

Jess: People expect me to say the big concerts, and they are fun. But for me it’s the small gigs in tiny clubs, where you can see everyone’s faces and chat to them afterwards. That’s when you really feel close to the audience.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to young musicians?

Jess: Practise, obviously. But more than that, play with other people as often as you can. You can practise alone in your bedroom for years, but you only really improve when you have to listen to other musicians.

Interviewer: Jess Moran, thank you.
